1. Why this lesson matters
Python is useful only when it makes an analysis clearer, repeatable and testable. This lesson
adds one analyst-sized skill and keeps the same evidence-first reasoning you already use in
Excel, SQL and Power BI.
2. What you are learning
- Understand the notebook/code/output mental model. - Install a stable environment and verify
it. - Run cells in order and restart/run-all before delivery.
3. What you already need / prerequisite
No Python/Jupyter skill is assumed.
4. Picture it in your head
Think of a notebook as a transparent lab notebook: explanation, code and output sit together.
Restart + Run All is like asking a new analyst to reproduce the work from page one with no
memory of what you clicked earlier.

Notebook = document with markdown/code/output cells. Kernel = Python process executing
cells. Hidden state = variable/import created by an earlier manual run but not reproducible from
notebook order. Environment = Python + installed packages/interpreter.

A notebook mixes explanation and executable code. That is useful for analysis because another
person can see not only the result, but how you obtained it. A reproducible notebook should run
from the first cell to the last without depending on hidden state. A cell that works only because
you ran some forgotten cell earlier is not a reliable analysis. Worked pattern: import sys

print(matplotlib.__version__)

have evidence of what runtime was used. Validation expectation: Save

Installing packages repeatedly without checking interpreter; cells work only because earlier

1. Why this lesson matters
Python is useful only when it makes an analysis clearer, repeatable and testable. This lesson
adds one analyst-sized skill and keeps the same evidence-first reasoning you already use in
Excel, SQL and Power BI.
2. What you are learning
- Separate detection from correction. - Clean text and dates transparently. - Treat duplicates,
missing data and invalid values using business rules.
3. What you already need / prerequisite
Prerequisite: PY2 plus the earlier analyst reasoning. The new Python/pandas operation is still
introduced from first principles.
4. Picture it in your head
Cleaning is an evidence-preserving repair bench: first mark the problem, then decide
whether/how to repair it. Never sweep a suspicious row away merely because a warning
disappears.
5. New words before we use them
Detection = identify issue without changing it. Correction = justified change. `duplicated()` =
duplicate flag. `pd.to_datetime(..., errors='coerce')` = invalid parse becomes missing/NaT. Issue
log = evidence of problem, decision and impact.

PY3 - Follow with me once
7. Follow with me once - fully worked teacher demonstration
Cleaning is not 'make warnings disappear.' Preserve evidence, identify the rule, investigate
impact and document the decision. Use .str.strip() for whitespace, pd.to_datetime(...,
errors='coerce') when you want invalid date text to become visible as missing, duplicated() for
duplicate detection, and explicit range/rule checks for invalid values. Worked pattern: work =
sales.copy() work["customer_id"] = work["customer_id"].astype("string").str.strip()
work["region"] = work["region"].astype("string").str.strip().str.title() work["order_date"] =
pd.to_datetime(work["order_date"], errors="coerce") duplicate_lines =
work[work.duplicated("order_line_id", keep=False)] bad_discount =
work.loc[~work["discount"].between(0,1)]
8. What you should see / be able to say
`errors='coerce'` does not fix a bad date. It exposes values that could not be parsed so you can
investigate them. Validation expectation: Save shape/key/type/count/total evidence appropriate
to the lesson. A cell running without an error is not by itself validation.
9. Why it worked
The code expresses a stated business/data rule and leaves objective evidence—shape, dtype,
key, row count, unmatched count, grouped reconciliation, saved output or clean rerun. A cell
running without an exception is not proof of correctness.
10. Common beginner mistakes
Blanket `dropna()`/`drop_duplicates()`; `fillna(0)` changing business meaning; overwriting raw
DataFrame; coercing invalid dates then treating them as fixed; deleting both/one duplicate
without stating the key/grain rule.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
If cleaning reduces row count unexpectedly, compare before/after counts and isolate the exact
rule. Never use dropna/drop_duplicates until you can name the business reason. Concept hint ->
file/column/API hint -> partial skeleton -> protected review after a saved attempt -> close review
and complete a changed retry.

7. Follow with me once - fully worked teacher demonstration
groupby changes grain. If you group by region, one output row represents one region. If you
group by month and category, each output row represents one month-category combination.
Always check whether a metric is additive at that grain. Counts, distinct counts and averages
answer different questions. Worked pattern: summary = ( work.groupby("region", dropna=False)
.agg( rows=("order_line_id","size"), orders=("order_id","nunique"),
net_sales=("net_sales","sum") ) .reset_index() )
8. What you should see / be able to say
`rows` and `orders` are different metrics. Grouping changes result grain, so you must know
whether you are counting lines or distinct orders. Validation expectation: Save
shape/key/type/count/total evidence appropriate to the lesson. A cell running without an error is
not by itself validation.
9. Why it worked
The code expresses a stated business/data rule and leaves objective evidence—shape, dtype,
key, row count, unmatched count, grouped reconciliation, saved output or clean rerun. A cell
running without an exception is not proof of correctness.
10. Common beginner mistakes
Confusing row count with distinct orders; grouping by wrong columns; averaging
already-aggregated numbers carelessly; not reconciling additive totals after grouping.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
If totals look wrong, state input grain and output grain, then reconcile the grouped sum to the
ungrouped total. Distinguish row count from nunique business entities. Concept hint ->
file/column/API hint -> partial skeleton -> protected review after a saved attempt -> close review

1. Why this lesson matters
Python is useful only when it makes an analysis clearer, repeatable and testable. This lesson
adds one analyst-sized skill and keeps the same evidence-first reasoning you already use in
Excel, SQL and Power BI.
2. What you are learning
- Choose join keys intentionally. - Detect one-to-many risks before merging. - Validate row counts

3. What you already need / prerequisite

introduced from first principles.
4. Picture it in your head
A merge is a controlled bridge between tables. `validate=` checks whether the bridge shape
matches your assumption; `indicator=True` shows which rows crossed and which did not.
5. New words before we use them
Merge = combine DataFrames on keys. `validate='many_to_one'` = assert right key uniqueness
for fact-to-dimension enrichment. `indicator=True` = create `_merge` source-status column.
Unmatched = key absent on other side. Concat = stack/align objects.

PY5 - Follow with me once
7. Follow with me once - fully worked teacher demonstration
A merge is the Python equivalent of a relational join. It can silently multiply rows if the right-side
key is not unique. Before a many-to-one enrichment merge, test the dimension key for
duplicates. During merge, `validate='many_to_one'` makes pandas raise an error if the assumed
relationship is false. `indicator=True` exposes unmatched rows. Worked pattern: products =
pd.read_csv("Practice_Data/products.csv") assert not products["product_id"].duplicated().any()
merged = work.merge( products, on="product_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one",
indicator=True ) print(merged["_merge"].value_counts()) print(len(work), len(merged))
8. What you should see / be able to say
`validate='many_to_one'` is a correctness control. `_merge` tells you which transaction keys did
not match the master. Validation expectation: Save shape/key/type/count/total evidence
appropriate to the lesson. A cell running without an error is not by itself validation.
9. Why it worked
The code expresses a stated business/data rule and leaves objective evidence—shape, dtype,
key, row count, unmatched count, grouped reconciliation, saved output or clean rerun. A cell
running without an exception is not proof of correctness.
10. Common beginner mistakes
Removing `validate=` when it raises; cleaning key values after merge instead of before;
duplicate dimension key silently multiplying fact rows; dropping `left_only` without investigation;
pandas null-key matching assumed identical to SQL behavior.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
If merge validation fails, stop and inspect duplicate keys on each side. Do not remove validate=
to make the error disappear. Concept hint -> file/column/API hint -> partial skeleton -> protected
review after a saved attempt -> close review and complete a changed retry.
